name: Plant
summary: Materials that come from plants: fruit, grain, wood, bast and leaf fibres, resins, and the cloth and paper made from them.

materials.name: Agar
materials.summary: A seaweed gel that sets firm and stays firm when warm; it allows a hot jelly.
materials.photo: a firm translucent clear agar jelly cube

materials.name: Sodium alginate
materials.summary: A salt from brown seaweed that sets in contact with calcium: the gel skin of spherification.
materials.photo: sodium alginate

materials.name: Lecithin
materials.summary: An emulsifier from egg yolk or soy; it holds the light airs of the modernist kitchen.
materials.photo: lecithin

materials.name: Kombu
materials.summary: Kelp dried in the sun; with katsuobushi it makes dashi, the base stock of Japan. Rich in glutamate.
materials.photo: kombu

materials.name: Seaweed
materials.photo: seaweed

materials.name: Cork
materials.summary: A bark used for the stoppers and lids of storage jars.
materials.photo: a square sample sheet of cork

materials.name: Oilskin
materials.summary: Cloth soaked in linseed oil for sailors and fishermen; Helly Hansen sold oiled linen in Norway from 1877.
materials.photo: a folded swatch of oilskin

materials.name: Waxed cotton
materials.summary: A dense cotton with a paraffin-wax finish that replaced linseed oil; it does not go stiff in the cold. The cloth of the country jacket.
materials.photo: a folded swatch of waxed cotton

materials.name: Wine
materials.summary: For deglazing, braising and sauce reduction.

materials.name: Olive oil
materials.summary: The fat of the south: raw, for frying and for confit.
materials.photo: olive oil

materials.name: Dashi
materials.summary: Stock of kombu and katsuobushi; its umami taught French chefs a lighter base.
materials.photo: a clear pale golden dashi broth in a small white bowl

materials.name: Vinegar
materials.summary: Wine or cider made sour by acetic bacteria; the sauce acid of the North.
materials.photo: vinegar

materials.name: Banana
materials.photo: a single ripe yellow banana
materials.summary: The long, curved fruit of the banana plant: a yellow peel around soft, sweet, starchy flesh. People eat it raw, fried, steamed or dried.

materials.name: Berries
materials.summary: Lingonberry, cloudberry, sea buckthorn, bilberry, raspberry and strawberry, wild or grown.
materials.photo: a small heap of mixed fresh berries: red lingonberries, orange cloudberries, blue bilberries, raspberries and strawberries

materials.name: Bitter orange
materials.summary: The orange of duck à l'orange and marmalade; the sweet orange came later, after 1500.
materials.photo: bitter orange

materials.name: Grape
materials.summary: Eaten fresh, dried, pressed for verjuice or made into wine.
materials.photo: grape

materials.name: Lemon
materials.summary: The Arabs grew lemons in Sicily and Spain; the acid of fish dishes and sauces.
materials.photo: lemon

materials.name: Lime
materials.summary: The Spanish took limes to the Americas, where they cure ceviche.
materials.photo: lime

materials.name: Olive
materials.photo: olive

materials.name: Orchard fruit
materials.summary: Apple, pear, quince, plum and cherry from orchards.
materials.photo: a group of orchard fruit: a red apple, a green pear, a yellow quince, purple plums and red cherries

materials.name: Peach
materials.summary: The Romans called it the Persian apple; pêche Melba of 1893 used it.
materials.photo: peach

materials.name: Plantain (cooking banana)
materials.photo: two green plantains
materials.summary: A starchy cooking banana. It is fried, boiled or steamed while green or ripe, and is a staple of West Africa, the Caribbean and Latin America.

materials.name: Tropical fruit
materials.summary: Pineapple, mango, passion fruit and papaya; Europe grew pineapples in hothouses from the 1700s.
materials.photo: tropical fruit

materials.name: Verjuice
materials.summary: The sour juice of unripe grapes; the acid of the medieval sauce before lemon and vinegar.
materials.photo: a small clear glass bottle of pale green-yellow verjuice

materials.name: Yuzu
materials.summary: A sour aromatic citrus of Japan; French chefs took it up in the 1990s.
materials.photo: yuzu

materials.name: Charcoal
materials.photo: a rough block of charcoal

materials.name: Bread
materials.summary: Flat bread from about 14,000 years ago; the medieval kitchen thickened sauces with it and served food on trenchers.
materials.photo: bread

materials.name: Maize
materials.summary: Domesticated from teosinte; nixtamalised with lime for masa. Columbus took it to Spain.
materials.photo: maize

materials.name: Quinoa
materials.summary: The seed of the Andean highlands; it reached European shops only in the late twentieth century.
materials.photo: quinoa

materials.name: Rice
materials.summary: Asian rice reached Spain with the Moors; paella and risotto came later. Short grain for sushi and risotto.
materials.photo: rice

materials.name: Rye
materials.summary: A hardy grain of the cold north; the dark sour bread of Scandinavia, Germany and Russia.
materials.photo: a small heap of long slender grey-green rye grains

materials.name: Wheat
materials.summary: Einkorn and emmer were sown in the Near East; bread wheat followed. Flour is the base of bread, pastry, roux and pasta.
materials.photo: wheat

materials.name: Bamboo
materials.photo: a square sample board of bamboo

materials.name: Sugar cane
materials.photo: sugar cane

materials.name: Coriander leaf
materials.summary: The leaf herb of Asian and Latin American cooking; the seed is a separate spice.
materials.photo: coriander leaf

materials.name: Fines herbes
materials.summary: Parsley, chervil, chives and tarragon, chopped fine; the herb mix of the French kitchen.
materials.photo: fines herbes

materials.name: Tarragon
materials.summary: The herb of béarnaise sauce and of poulet à l'estragon.
materials.photo: a bunch of fresh tarragon sprigs with long narrow smooth green leaves

materials.name: Thyme and bay
materials.summary: With parsley, the bouquet garni of stocks and braises.
materials.photo: a sprig of fresh thyme with tiny leaves beside two dark green bay leaves

materials.name: Wild plants and flowers
materials.summary: Foraged leaves, flowers, berries, moss and needles; the base of the foraging kitchen.
materials.photo: wild plants and flowers

materials.name: Bobbin lace
materials.summary: Lace plaited from threads on many bobbins over a pattern on a pillow; Flanders and the Low Countries led it.
materials.photo: a folded swatch of bobbin lace

materials.name: Leavers lace
materials.summary: Machine lace from the Leavers frame; it made lace a cloth of the middle class and of lingerie.
materials.photo: a folded swatch of leavers lace

materials.name: Needle lace
materials.summary: Lace built from buttonhole stitches with a needle; Venetian 'punto in aria' was the lace of the ruff and the collar.
materials.photo: a folded swatch of needle lace

materials.name: Rubberised cloth
materials.summary: Two cotton cloths glued with naphtha-dissolved rubber; the first waterproof coat cloth, and the name of the coat.
materials.photo: a folded swatch of rubberised cloth

materials.name: Crepe rubber
materials.summary: Raw latex rolled into crinkled sheets for a soft, grippy sole; the sole of the desert boot and the creeper.
materials.photo: a square sheet of honey-brown crinkled crepe rubber, a crepe shoe sole

materials.name: Natural rubber
materials.summary: Latex from the rubber tree; the Olmec made rubber balls. Raw rubber goes soft in heat and hard in cold.
materials.photo: a square sheet of translucent amber-brown natural rubber

materials.name: Banana leaf
materials.photo: a single folded fresh green banana leaf
materials.summary: The large, waxy leaf of the banana plant. Cooks wrap food in it to steam or grill it, and in South India it is the plate.

materials.name: Pulses
materials.summary: Lentil, chickpea, bean and pea: the protein of the plant kitchen.

materials.name: Tofu
materials.summary: Curd of soy milk pressed into blocks; the protein of the Buddhist kitchen.

materials.name: Banana plant (Musa)

materials.summary: A large herb of the genus Musa. Its stem is a pseudostem of rolled leaf bases; it gives fruit, leaves and fibre.

materials.name: Flax plant
materials.photo: a bunch of flax plants with slender stems, small blue flowers and round seed bolls

materials.name: Abacá (Manila hemp)
materials.photo: a loose bundle of long straight cream abaca fibre strands, unspun
materials.summary: The fibre of Musa textilis, also called Manila hemp. It is strong and resists salt water, so it makes rope, paper and woven hats.

materials.name: Banana fibre (bashōfu)
materials.photo: a loose hank of pale banana fibre
materials.summary: Fibre from the pseudostem of the banana plant. In Okinawa it is woven into bashōfu cloth.

materials.name: Cane and bamboo
materials.summary: Woven cane or bamboo for the overhead handles of teapots and kettles.

materials.name: Cotton
materials.summary: Cotton threads at Mehrgarh and cloth at Mohenjo-daro; Peru grew a second species from about 4500 BC.
materials.photo: a loose hank of cotton fibre

materials.name: Flax (linen)
materials.summary: Linen cloth from flax is in Egyptian graves of about 5000 BC; dyed wild flax fibres from a cave in Georgia are about 30,000 years old.
materials.photo: a loose bundle of long silky pale grey-blond flax fibre strands, unspun line flax

materials.name: Hemp
materials.summary: Hemp cloth is in Chinese graves of the third millennium BC; Europe used it for sailcloth, rope and work clothes.
materials.photo: a loose hank of hemp fibre

materials.name: Black pepper
materials.summary: The most traded spice of the ancient world; Rome bought it by the tonne.
materials.photo: black pepper

materials.name: Chilli pepper
materials.summary: Capsicum went from the Americas round the world in fifty years: to Hungary, India, Sichuan and Korea.
materials.photo: chilli pepper

materials.name: Cinnamon
materials.summary: Bark of the cinnamon tree; the base of the medieval cameline sauce.
materials.photo: cinnamon

materials.name: Clove
materials.summary: Dried flower buds from the Spice Islands; studs the onion of a classic stock.
materials.photo: clove

materials.name: Cocoa
materials.summary: Ground cacao beans drunk with chilli; Europe added sugar.
materials.photo: cocoa

materials.name: Ginger
materials.summary: A rhizome used dried in medieval Europe and fresh in Asia.
materials.photo: ginger

materials.name: Grains of paradise
materials.summary: A peppery seed from the Guinea coast; a medieval spice that nearly left the kitchen.
materials.photo: a small heap of tiny glossy red-brown pyramid-shaped grains of paradise seeds

materials.name: Nutmeg and mace
materials.summary: Seed and aril of one tree; in béchamel and the medieval spice mix.
materials.photo: nutmeg and mace

materials.name: Saffron
materials.summary: Stigmas of the crocus; it coloured medieval dishes gold. Used now in risotto and bouillabaisse.
materials.photo: saffron

materials.name: Vanilla
materials.summary: Totonac people cured the pod of an orchid; the hand pollination of 1841 by Edmond Albius made it a crop.
materials.photo: vanilla

materials.name: Cane sugar
materials.summary: Crystal sugar reached Europe through the crusades; a costly spice until the plantations.
materials.photo: cane sugar

materials.name: Artichoke
materials.summary: Bred from the cardoon in Sicily and Naples; Catherine de' Medici took it to France.
materials.photo: artichoke

materials.name: Asparagus
materials.summary: Cato described its culture; white asparagus is grown in the dark under earth.
materials.photo: asparagus

materials.name: Cabbage
materials.summary: Kale, cabbage, cauliflower and broccoli are one species, bred in Europe.
materials.photo: cabbage

materials.name: Carrot
materials.summary: Purple and yellow at first; the orange carrot was bred in the Netherlands in the seventeenth century.
materials.photo: carrot

materials.name: Garlic
materials.summary: Used raw, confit or roasted; the mark of Provençal and southern cooking.
materials.photo: garlic

materials.name: Leek
materials.summary: A soft onion for soups and vichyssoise; the white is the part used.
materials.photo: leek

materials.name: Onion
materials.summary: The base of most savoury cooking, sweated, browned or raw.
materials.photo: onion

materials.name: Potato
materials.summary: Thousands of Andean kinds; Parmentier made it French food after 1772. Pommes purée, frites and chuño.
materials.photo: potato

materials.name: Root vegetables
materials.summary: Turnip, swede, celeriac, beetroot and parsnip: the winter store of the north.
materials.photo: a group of root vegetables: a purple-topped turnip, a swede, a celeriac, a red beetroot and a parsnip

materials.name: Young greens and shoots
materials.summary: Pea shoots, young leaves, wild garlic and small salad leaves picked young.

materials.name: Shallot
materials.summary: A mild onion of the French sauce: beurre blanc, béarnaise and bordelaise start with it.
materials.photo: shallot

materials.name: Tomato
materials.summary: Mattioli recorded the pomi d'oro in 1544; the first Italian tomato sauce recipe is of 1692.

materials.name: Oxford cloth
materials.summary: A basket weave with a soft hand; Scottish mills named shirtings after universities. The cloth of the button-down shirt.
materials.photo: a folded swatch of oxford cloth

materials.name: Waffle weave
materials.photo: a folded swatch of waffle weave

materials.name: Corduroy
materials.summary: A weft-pile cloth with cut cords ('wales'); the cloth of country trousers and the 1970s jacket.
materials.photo: a folded swatch of corduroy

materials.name: Terry towelling
materials.summary: A loop-pile cloth that Henry Christy saw in Turkey and his mill made by machine; the cloth of robes and sweatbands.
materials.photo: a folded swatch of terry towelling

materials.name: Book cloth
materials.photo: a folded swatch of book cloth

materials.name: Calico
materials.summary: A plain cotton from the Malabar coast; England banned printed calico imports in 1700 and 1721 to protect wool and silk weavers.
materials.photo: a folded swatch of calico

materials.name: Cambric (batiste)
materials.summary: A fine, dense plain weave for shirts, collars, handkerchiefs and lingerie, named after the town of Cambrai.
materials.photo: a folded swatch of cambric

materials.name: Canvas and duck
materials.summary: A heavy plain weave for sails, tents, work coats and the upper of the first sneakers.
materials.photo: a folded swatch of canvas and duck

materials.name: Elastic webbing
materials.summary: A narrow woven band with rubber or elastane core threads; it forms the waistband, the strap and the leg band. Thomas Hancock patented rubber elastic for garments in 1820.
materials.photo: a folded swatch of elastic webbing

materials.name: Gingham
materials.summary: A yarn-dyed check in white and one colour; the name comes from a Malay word for striped cloth.
materials.photo: a folded swatch of gingham

materials.name: Glazed chintz
materials.summary: A printed or painted cotton with a glazed surface; the East India companies brought it to Europe in the 17th century.
materials.photo: a folded swatch of glazed chintz

materials.name: Linen
materials.photo: a folded swatch of linen

materials.name: Linen cloth
materials.summary: The oldest cloth of dress; cool, crisp and quick to crease. Shirts, summer suits and underwear were linen until cotton took over.
materials.photo: a folded swatch of linen cloth

materials.name: Muslin
materials.summary: A fine, open cotton of hand-spun yarn from Dhaka; the name comes from Mosul. It was the cloth of the Empire-line dress after 1795.
materials.photo: a folded swatch of muslin

materials.name: Percale
materials.photo: a folded swatch of percale

materials.name: Poplin
materials.summary: A plain weave with a fine weft rib; the name may come from 'papeline', the cloth of the papal town of Avignon. The cloth of the dress shirt.
materials.photo: a folded swatch of poplin

materials.name: Seersucker
materials.summary: Two warps at different tension make puckered stripes that stand off the skin; the name comes from Persian 'milk and sugar'.
materials.photo: a folded swatch of blue and white striped seersucker cotton with puckered stripes

materials.name: Ventile
materials.summary: A dense weave of long-staple cotton that swells when wet and keeps out water; made for the immersion suits of RAF pilots.
materials.photo: a folded swatch of ventile

materials.name: Chino twill
materials.summary: A light cotton twill of US army trousers in the Philippines; the name comes from the Chinese cloth. It went to the campus after 1945.
materials.photo: a folded swatch of chino twill

materials.name: Coutil
materials.summary: A dense cotton twill, often in a herringbone weave, that resists the pull of the bones; the standard cloth of corset bodies.
materials.photo: a folded swatch of coutil

materials.name: Denim
materials.summary: A warp-faced twill with an indigo warp and a white weft; 'serge de Nîmes'. Levi Strauss and Jacob Davis patented the riveted work trouser in 1873.
materials.photo: a folded swatch of denim

materials.name: Khaki drill
materials.summary: A cotton twill dyed the colour of dust ('khaki' in Urdu) for the Corps of Guides; armies took it for field dress.
materials.photo: a folded swatch of khaki drill
